Hong Leong Holdings completes office tower revamp and digital integration of business operations
article:
Hong Leong Holdings , the private property arm of Hong Leong Group Singapore, has completed a twin transformation programme involving the revitalisation of Hong Leong Building and the digital integration of its core business operations.

Together, the initiatives strengthen the developer’s operational efficiency, sustainability performance and long-term resilience, the company said in a Nov 25 release.

Both initiatives were carried out at a total cost of over $40 million.

The renewal of Hong Leong Building, a 45-storey commercial tower at 16 Raffles Quay that was built in 1976, involved a comprehensive asset enhancement initiative centred around adaptive reuse.

About 95% of the 158m-tall tower’s existing structure and original granite façade was retained, while key amenities, common spaces and infrastructure were upgraded. The latter includes a refreshed podium frontage, enhanced common areas and lift lobbies, and a new drop-off point to improve accessibility.

Hong Leong Building is now BCA Green Mark Platinum-certified, the highest tier under Singapore’ national green building rating system.

On the digital front, Hong Leong Holdings established an integrated operating platform that connects the developers’ sales, leasing and finance functions.  The new platform provides a unified view of data from all three functions across the company’s residential and commercial businesses.

The roll-out has resulted in data visibility and accuracy improving by 30%, while operational efficiency has been enhanced by up to 65%, said Hong Leong Holdings.

The digital transformation was carried out in collaboration with advisor PwC Singapore and technology partners Showsuite, SAP and Planon Asia.

The transformation programme, which began in October 2023, strengthens both the company’s physical assets and business capabilities, said Quek Kon Hui, Hong Leong Holdings executive director.

“Together, they advance our sustainability ambitions, enhance business resilience and position us for the future, creating long-term value for our stakeholders,” he added.

title: First Fila 'sport-fashion hotel' opens in Shanghai; Andaz debuts in Australia with Gold Coast property
article:
Hyatt Asia Pacific has broadened its Asia Pacific portfolio with two new properties in Shanghai, China and Gold Coast Australia.

In China,  Fila House Shanghai — the world’s first Fila-branded ‘sport-fashion hotel’ — opened on Nov 13, Hyatt said in a Nov 24 release.

The hotel is located in Shanghai Anta Center,  the global innovation hub and corporate campus for Chinese sportswear giant Anta Group. The group holds the rights to operate the Fila brand in China, Hong Kong and Macao.

The property is part of Hyatt’s JdV portfolio, comprising a global collection of independent boutique hotels.

Fila House Shanghai has 108 rooms and suites. The suites feature design themes based on the sportswear brand’s golf, tennis and athletic lines.

The biggest suite at the hotel, the 196 sq m (2,110 sq ft) Biella Presidential Suite, is designed around Fila’s signature red, navy and white palette, while also celebrating the brand’s Italian heritage. It includes a private terrace overlooking cityscape and park views.

Amenities at Fila House Shanghai include the Pure Wellness & Activity Space on the third floor. It features a fitness club, an activity pool, and indoor swimming pool, alongside group training spaces, yoga and Pilates studios, changing and shower facilities, and relaxation and recovery areas.

The hotel has two restaurants: 1911 Ristorante and Privato. The former, named after the year Fila was founded, is an all-day restaurant offering Italian and Mediterranean cuisine through an à la carte buffet concept.

The latter offers Fujian and Cantonese cuisine, with a focus on seasoned ingredients and thoughtful presentation.

In Australia, Andaz Gold Coast opened on Nov 16. It marks the country’s first Andaz property.

The 202-room hotel is located in Broadbeach within The Star Gold Coast integrated resorts and entertainment precinct. It was designed by Australian architecture firm DBI Architects, with interiors by design studio Hachem.

The hotel features four dining destinations, with a highlight being Nove Restaurant and Bar, which features fire-led Mediterranean cooking and interiors designed by MAS Architecture Studio.

Another highlight is the hotel’s signature experiences, which include poolside Pilate and breathwork sessions, barbecue evenings on selected Thursdays, and a daily Golden Hour, which offers in-house guests complimentary beverages and snacks in the evening.

title: More than number crunchers: How quantity surveyors are gearing up for the future of building
article:
Suppose you inherit an old landed house and decide to undertake a major renovation to turn it into your family home.

You engage an architect, settle on the design and agree to a contractor’s quotation of $400,000. However, the contractual terms are loosely defined, with no firm completion date.

The renovation progresses more slowly than expected. Halfway through the works, the contractor unexpectedly revises the cost to $600,000.

Where will you find the additional $200,000? What assurance is there that the renovation will be completed on time without further cost overruns?

This is a scenario that Colin Kin, president of the quantity surveying division of the Singapore Institute of Surveyors and Valuers (SISV), says happens all too often and illustrates the importance of cost planning and contract management.

Had a quantity surveyor been involved from the outset, the homeowner would have received a detailed breakdown of the estimated costs, from windows and doors to floor finishes and bathroom fittings.

The quantity surveyor could also have worked with the architect to keep the design within budget while helping the owner negotiate clear terms with the contractor — such as payment schedules, changes to the works, completion deadlines and penalties for delays.

"Most people are already familiar with what architects, engineers and contractors do," says Kin, who is also managing director of Rider Levett Bucknall (RLB) in Singapore.

"But there's this unseen profession that nobody ever considers if you're outside of the built-environment sector. Somebody needs to take care of the costs and the contracts."

Natalie Yong, first vice-president of SISV's quantity surveying division, also recognises the financial and emotional significance of building or renovating a home, where families may spend many years of their lives.

"If you're going to live there, you want to feel good about your home. You don't want to think, 'Wow, it cost me so much. I overpaid for this,'" says Yong, managing director of LCH Quantity Surveying.

What quantity surveyors do, and what's next

Quantity surveyors keep building projects on time, on target and on budget throughout the lifecycle — from the design stage to tendering and construction.

They are often described as part lawyer, part accountant and part project adviser, though the value they bring is not always well understood.

Their clients can range from homeowners undertaking extensive renovations or rebuilds to property developers building condos and hotels.

Quantity surveyors also work on public-sector and infrastructure projects such as HDB developments, hospitals, MRT stations, roads and airports. On the construction side, contractors may engage these professionals to prepare tender bids, manage costs and handle payment claims.

Limited awareness of quantity surveying as a career has made attracting new talent a challenge, while the profession also faces difficulties retaining experienced practitioners.

In February, the Building and Construction Authority set up a dedicated QS Workgroup to examine these issues and future-proof the profession.

In September, the workgroup came up with recommendations to attract, develop and retain quantity surveyors, and help firms operate more efficiently and profitably.

"As projects become larger and more complex, the future of quantity surveying must be about greater value and taking on more strategic roles in project delivery," said Second Minister for Finance and National Development Indranee Rajah when announcing the workgroup's recommendations.

'Count every dollar, make every dollar count'

Long before construction workers arrive on site, quantity surveyors are already working out what a building will cost and whether it is financially viable.

They calculate the cost of essentially every aspect of a building — from structural elements and façades to interior finishes.

These calculations then form the basis of cost estimates, feasibility studies and pre-tender estimates, which help clients set realistic budgets, and guide architects and engineers in designing within those limits.

They also evaluate contractors' bids and prepare contracts that set out costs, timelines and responsibilities.

Once construction kicks off, they monitor expenditure, assess the cost of changes and verify payments for work done.

"A quantity surveyor also looks at value engineering, finding ways to cut waste in a building, whether in productivity or sustainability," notes Eugene Seah, second vice-president of SISV's quantity surveying division and CEO of DLS Consultancy.

The aim is to achieve the best value for money, which does not always mean choosing the cheapest option.

"Count every dollar and make every dollar count," as Kin puts it.

Developers typically set their construction budgets with target profit margins in mind, based on the expected selling prices of their units.

That means quantity surveyors must work closely with other consultants to stick to the budget.

"If we go over that fixed budget target, the developer is not going to make money because their selling prices can't be increased much," Kin says.

The bigger picture in creating value

Besides keeping construction costs in check, quantity surveyors also assess how much a building will cost to operate and maintain over time.

They often take into account the durability of materials and equipment, energy consumption, disposal and replacement costs.

This process, known as life-cycle costing, helps determine whether spending more now could be more economical in the long run.

Kin cites the example of a hotel owner who wants to install thick, luxurious carpets expected to last 15 years. However, given the heavy foot traffic in a hotel, the carpets may need replacing after just five years.

"Maybe you don't need to spend so much money on a thick carpet. You can choose a cheaper, medium-grade one that can be replaced more regularly to keep it looking fresh," he suggests.

"We look at which option is the most efficient from a cost-to-use perspective. It's not about just choosing the cheapest one but which will give the biggest bang for buck," Kin adds.

Quantity surveyors can also use their knowledge of construction methods, technology, materials and design to identify alternative solutions that reduce costs, speed up construction and improve overall project outcomes.

Seah recalls a building that was initially designed with three basement levels to house a certain number of carpark lots.

Drawing on his experience with other developments, he suggested incorporating the parking spaces into the ramp linking the basement levels: "Why can't the ramp be the car park itself?"

This improved the car park's space efficiency, reducing the average floor area required per parking lot by about 15.6%.

He notes that the client saved $8 million by building two basements instead of three, while still having the same number of carpark lots. The project was also completed more quickly.

"Quantity surveyors can add a lot of value once they understand design and technology, and bring all these together instead of having people working in silos. It's not just fixated on cost," Seah says.

A stronger voice at the table

Identifying ways to improve a project is one thing, but having the confidence and communication skills to convey those ideas effectively is another.

Yong observes that quantity surveyors tend to be “the quietest people” during meetings with clients and other consultants. "Many don't speak up," she adds.

She believes this needs to change — quantity surveyors have to become more vocal, navigate difficult conversations and take on a greater advisory role.

This comes as AI is taking over more of the profession’s routine work, such as calculating quantities and analysing cost data.

"The quantity surveyor has to exercise professional judgement. Our experience in handling many kinds of projects enables us to have a more nuanced view on how to proceed," Yong says.

"AI can give you data and point out discrepancies, but it can't decide for you and tell you how to diagnose it. You need to apply judgement and advise the client," she continues.

Agreeing that having a human in the loop will remain important, Seah sees the profession taking on a bigger role in bringing together architects, engineers, contractors and other stakeholders.

This requires quantity surveyors to interpret information, express themselves clearly and help clients understand the implications of each decision, Seah highlights.

Kin describes quantity surveyors as increasingly becoming "skilled negotiators, communicators, integrators and peacemakers" who can empathise with different stakeholders, anticipate potential disputes and find solutions.

He adds that quantity surveyors are also equipped to manage uncertainty, from changing requirements to unforeseen costs and risks.

"Dealing with flexibility and unknowns, contingency management — that’s not something you can give to AI," Kin notes.

Getting on students' radar

Despite hundreds of entry-level vacancies available in quantity surveying, many students are unfamiliar with it as a career option.

There were about 320 such vacancies in March 2026, according to Ministry of Manpower data cited in the QS Workgroup report.

However, Singapore has no dedicated degree or diploma programme on quantity surveying.

The National University of Singapore (NUS) recently introduced a new specialisation in Contract Management and Cost Engineering, within its Bachelor of Engineering (Infrastructure and Project Management) undergraduate programme.

Another pathway is the existing Bachelor of Building and Project Management programme at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, which offers training relevant to quantity surveying.

SISV has also stepped up its outreach efforts, including organising a competition with the NUS Department of Built Environment earlier this year. More than 60 students from polytechnics, junior colleges and International Baccalaureate explored cost, contracts and sustainability at the three-day challenge.

Yong hopes such initiatives will raise awareness of the career path and attract more students with a diverse range of interests and strengths.

"Every time I interview a candidate and ask why they studied quantity surveying, 90% of the time they answer, 'My maths is very good,'" she says.

While mathematical aptitude is essential, the profession also draws on a broad set of skills, including communication, negotiation and collaboration.

Yong also believes existing quantity surveyors can do more to encourage others to join the industry, by sharing what they find fulfilling about their work.

At the same time, part of the challenge in attracting talent may lie in the name "quantity surveyor" itself.

The QS Workgroup has recommended reviewing the title to better reflect the profession’s broad and strategic role.

"How to rebrand ourselves such that the youth will find it appealing is the biggest challenge we have at the moment," says Kin. "If we say 'quantity surveyor', nobody knows what we do."

Ideas floated during brainstorming have included "commercial manager" and "cost and contracts professional", although no new name has been decided.

Retaining talent and supporting firms

While a rebrand could help attract new entrants, retaining talent also requires better remuneration, manageable workloads and clearer career progression.

The workgroup has suggested improving the financial sustainability of firms so they can invest more in staff development and technology.

Kin points out that quantity surveying firms are often paid a fee agreed on at the start of a project, even when delays and changes lead to substantial additional work later that they may not be paid for.

"We’re burning hours and burning resources, which affects profitability," Kin says.

"If you had said it'll be $1 million on day one but it ends up costing you $2 million, there's no way you can increase salaries or give bonuses that year."

To tackle this, SISV is developing a Value Articulation Framework — a comprehensive list of core and value-added services — that will help clients and quantity surveying firms better define the scope and complexity of services from the outset.

The aim is to make things more transparent and give firms a clearer basis for pricing their services and charging for additional work, Kin says.

Celebrating those behind the scenes

Recognising the achievements of quantity surveyors could help build professional pride, raise the prestige of the profession and inspire the next generation to join the industry.

The QS Workgroup recommends both public- and private-sector clients to recognise firms’ exemplary contributions, be it at annual dinners, on digital platforms or through other channels.

Yong has often seen architects, engineers, landscape designers and other consultants recognised for their contributions at industry awards ceremonies, whereas quantity surveyors receive little to no mention.

"The [built environment] sector gives awards for the best architecture, engineering excellence for the most optimal columns and beams, and for landscaping of beautiful parks. But there’s nothing about quantity surveying," she remarks wryly.

She hopes such recognition will give younger professionals something to aspire to and help them feel valued for their contributions.

SISV is planning an awards ceremony for next year and has approached public agencies about recognising the profession's contributions.

Pride in the work and optimism for the future

Kin believes quantity surveyors have much to take pride in, especially the integrity, prudence and impartiality required when managing large sums of money.

"We deal with billions of dollars and ensure everything is above board and spent well, as stewards of value and stewards of public funds," he notes.

"When hospitals, HDB flats and MRT stations are built, we make sure taxpayers' hard-earned money is properly allocated. There is tremendous pride in that," Kin adds.

Meanwhile, Seah likens the profession's evolution to a metamorphosis, with a "blue ocean" of opportunities.

Having started his career using manual cut-and-shuffle methods and stencils, he is excited about the possibilities that digital technology and AI could open up.

"The next jump is going to be fantastic. But are we ready for it? That’s the question," Seah says, stressing the need to prepare both current and future generations of quantity surveyors for the shift.

For all the changes ahead, the three share an enduring enthusiasm for construction.

For Kin, part of the fascination comes from watching buildings take form from the ground up.

"When you go to a blank site, there's nothing there. Then they dig a hole, and they put in the piles, and you see this creation coming out of the ground,” he says.

"There's something magical about construction."

----------

Early sparks of a career in quantity surveying

Growing up, Eugene Seah found joy in assembling model aeroplanes and building things with Lego.

A third-generation quantity surveyor, he credits his grandfather — Seah Mong Hee, Asia’s first chartered quantity surveyor — and father, Seah Choo Meng, with nurturing his love for construction.

The young Seah began visiting construction sites at the age of eight and found satisfaction in watching buildings rise from the ground.

"I wanted to do something that makes a difference, where I can create value," says Seah, second vice-president of the quantity surveying (QS) division at the Singapore Institute of Surveyors and Valuers (SISV).

Even the most outstanding designs cannot be realised if the costs are prohibitive. "If it's too expensive and doesn’t make bankable sense, you can’t build it anyway," Seah adds.

Meanwhile, Natalie Yong, first vice-president of the QS division, had originally hoped to become an architect, but pursued quantity surveying when she was not accepted into architecture school.

With parents in the construction business, she had a headstart in the sector, traipsing to her first site at 14.

"I realised the underlying question was always, 'How much?' when my family was selling their products," she shares.

During her polytechnic years, Yong had an unusual weekend hobby: visiting condo showflats.

"I would study showflats and pore over their marketing materials, in and out. Seeing how things are being built also excites me," she adds.

As for Kin, his passion for construction began with a childhood storybook depicting a builder putting up a house from scratch, from laying the foundation and brick walls to installing the roof.

A knack for numbers later led him to discover that quantity surveying married two of his favourite subjects: construction and accounting.

"I just fell in love with my university course," says Kin, who was eager to start working after graduation. At SISV, he is now chairman of the central management committee and president of the QS division.

title: Million-dollar HDB flat deals may total up to 2,800 in 2027: Huttons
article:
Million-dollar HDB flat transactions are expected to reach between 2,400 and 2,800 in 2027, up from an estimated 2,100 this year, even as the wider resale market stays soft. The projections come from Huttons Data Analytics, the research and data division of Singapore real estate agency Huttons Asia.

The 2026 estimate is 31.7% higher than the 1,594 deals in 2025. Based on Huttons’ forecast, million-dollar flats made up about 8% of resale transactions this year, up from 6.1% the year before. Total HDB resale volume is estimated at 26,000 for 2026, similar to last year.

A wave of flats completing their five-year minimum occupation period (MOP) contributed to the rise in transactions of $1 million and above. More than 13,000 units fulfilled their MOP in 2026 — almost 70% higher than previous years — with about 60% located in mature estates such as Bedok, Queenstown and Toa Payoh.

The average price of million-dollar transaction stands at $1.16 million in 2026, based on HDB data downloaded as of Nov 19. The figure is 1% higher than $1.14 million in 2025.

By location, Toa Payoh, Queenstown and Bukit Merah recorded the most million-dollar deals in 2026.

Buyers are also favouring newer flats. Those aged four to six years made up 25% of million-dollar deals, five percentage points higher than in 2025.

Huttons said the newer, popular Build-To-Order projects that recently achieved their MOP include several developments in the Bidadari neighborhood in Toa Payoh, such as Alkaff Vista and Alkaff CourtView ; Bedok South Horizon in Bedok; and St George’s Towers in Kallang/Whampoa.

Other favoured projects were Northshore Straitsview in Punggol and SkyParc @ Dawson in Queenstown, where a five-room flat was sold for a record $1.818 million in October.

As these projects pre-date the Prime, Plus and Standard categorisations for HDB flats that were introduced in October 2024, they have fewer resale restrictions, Huttons noted. Prime and Plus flats have a 10-year MOP period, and are also subject to subsidy clawbacks upon resale.

Another 18,939 flats will meet their MOP requirement in 2027, with about 60% located in non-mature estates, a reversal from 2026. The top three towns with the highest number of flats fulfilling the five-year MOP are Yishun, Tampines and Punggol.

The strong pipeline of resale flat supply could thus continue to support million-dollar deals, according to Huttons.

For the wider HDB resale market, the firm forecasts prices to slip by 0.5% for 2026, in contrast to the 2.9% increase last year. This will mark the first decline since 2019.

Next year, overall HDB resale prices could bottom out and thus edge up by 0% to 2%, on an estimated 24,000 to 27,000 transactions, Huttons said.

But a raise is only as good as the money behind it.

because profits grew.
Others leaned on lower costs or one-off gains, and those raises rarely last.

Can STE keep raising its dividend?
STE is a global technology, defence and engineering group headquartered in Singapore.
Its third-quarter interim dividend of S$0.05 per share was 25% higher than the S$0.04 paid a year ago.
For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), STE has declared S$0.14, up from S$0.12.
The step-up came earlier: STE also paid S$0.05 in the second quarter.
A rule drives the increase.
From FY2026, STE’s new dividend policy pays out about one-third of each year’s increase in net profit as extra dividends.
The dividend grows only if profit does.
Is profit growing? STE won’t say until full-year results.
The group reports half-yearly and gives only business updates in the first and third quarters, so its 9M update carries no profit or cash flow figures.
Revenue offers the best clue.
It rose 10% year on year (YoY) to S$10.0 billion in 9M2026, or 13% excluding LeeBoy, a business STE divested on 4 September 2025.
The risk sits inside the formula.
If full-year profit stalls, the policy adds nothing to the dividend.
Why did DBS pay more while its profit fell?
DBS
declared a S$0.66 ordinary dividend for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), 10% more than the S$0.60 a year earlier.
It also declared a S$0.15 capital return dividend, unchanged from a year ago.
Together, the S$0.81 sits 8% above last year’s S$0.75.
The quarter itself was weaker.
Net profit fell 4.8% YoY to S$2.81 billion after markets trading non-interest income dropped to S$17 million from S$419 million.
Net interest margin narrowed from 1.96% to 1.87% as Singapore interest rates fell.
So why pay more? The core bank kept growing.
Commercial book income, which excludes trading, rose 4%, while customer loans grew 9.5% to S$478.58 billion.
Nine-month net profit reached a record S$8.82 billion, up 2%.
Here’s the thing: the ordinary dividend grew 10% while nine-month profit grew 2%.
In other words, DBS appears to be paying out a larger share of what it earns.
Its update gives no payout ratio, so that gap is worth watching.
For 2027, management expects total income growth in the mid-single-digit range.
CEO Tan Su Shan also warned that the outlook has become more uncertain, citing elevated energy prices, tighter financial conditions and geopolitical risks.
Is MLT’s 0.1% DPU increase worth anything?
MLT owns 172 logistics properties in nine markets.
Its distribution per unit (DPU) for 2QFY2027 was S$0.01816, up just 0.1% from S$0.01815 a year ago.
MLT’s fiscal year ends in March, so 2QFY2027 covers the three months to 30 September 2026.
The properties did better than the payout.
Net property income (NPI) rose 1.0% to S$154.8 million, helped by the redeveloped Mapletree Joo Koon Logistics Hub, acquisition in India and organic growth, mainly in Singapore.
A stronger renminbi and Australian dollar also helped, and currency gains can reverse.
Where did the rest go?
Distributions to perpetual securities holders rose 33.6% after MLT issued S$400 million of new perpetual securities ahead of a planned November 2026 redemption.
Carrying both issues at once is a cost that should ease once the old one is redeemed.
Other offsets look stickier.
MLT lost income from divested properties.
Portfolio rental reversion improved to 2.1%, but China stayed negative at -1.7%.
China, again, is the drag.
Aggregate leverage of 37.5% also flatters the balance sheet.
On a pro forma basis, it would have been 40.4%.
Get Smart: Measure the raise against what pays for it
Before you celebrate a higher payout, set its growth beside the growth of the money behind it.
At STE, a published rule ties the dividend to profit growth.
At DBS, the ordinary dividend grew 10% against nine-month profit growth of 2%.
At MLT, NPI grew 1.0% while DPU grew 0.1%, and costs took the difference.

title: Dividend Yield vs. Dividend Payout Ratio: What’s the Difference?
article:
Having covered
dividend basics
and compared
REITs and blue chips
in our first two guides, we turn to two key metrics every investor should understand.
Most beginners assume that a stock offering a 7% dividend yield is a better investment than one with a 4% yield.
This is a common rookie mistake – focusing solely on dividend yield because it shows you how much income you can receive.
However, a high dividend yield doesn’t tell you everything you need to know about a stock.
Experienced investors look beyond dividend yield and also examine the dividend payout ratio.
What Is Dividend Yield and How Do You Calculate It?
Dividend yield measures how much a company pays shareholders in annual dividends relative to its current share price.
If a stock trades at S$5 and pays annual dividends of S$0.25 per share, its dividend yield is 5%.
Even when the payouts remain unchanged, the yield can change with share price fluctuations.
If the share price falls to S$4 and annual dividends stay at S$0.25 per share, the yield rises to 6.25%.
Hence, yield alone is not a foolproof indicator of a good investment.
Dividend yields from the past are not an assurance of future dividends.
Companies can also reduce or suspend dividends without warning.
What Is Dividend Payout Ratio and Why Does It Matter?
The dividend payout ratio is the percentage of a company’s earnings that it distributes to shareholders as dividends.
Investors can tell how much of a company’s profit is paid to the shareholders and how much remains undistributed.
A company that earns S$0.50 per share and pays out S$0.25 per share in dividends will have a dividend payout ratio of 50%.
Singapore’s largest bank,
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05), paid out about 64% of its FY2025 earnings as ordinary dividends, or about 80% once its capital return dividends are included.
A sustainable payout ratio is generally considered to sit between 40% and 70%.
Earnings not paid out to shareholders can fund business expansion, repay debt or support other corporate purposes.
A company that consistently pays out a high share of its earnings might have less flexibility to manage unexpected challenges or sustain dividends during trying times.
Singapore real estate investment trusts (S-REITs), however, must distribute at least 90% of their taxable income to qualify for tax transparency.
Hence, REIT investors should focus on distribution-related metrics and
cash flow
instead.
Dividend Yield vs. Dividend Payout Ratio: Key Differences
Dividend yield and dividend payout ratio measure different aspects of a company’s dividend performance.

Dividend Payout Ratio
What it measures
Dividend income relative to share price
Dividends relative to earnings
Formula

Main purpose
Estimates income yield
Helps assess payout sustainability
Affected by
Share price and dividend changes
Earnings and dividend changes
Key concern
High yield may reflect a falling share price
High payout may leave little earnings buffer
Dividend yield helps investors assess potential dividend returns, whereas the payout ratio provides insight into dividend sustainability.
Neither metric should be used in isolation; investors should always consider the company’s financial health, such as cash flow, earnings stability, and debt levels before making investment decisions.
Can a Stock Have a High Dividend Yield but an Unsustainable Payout Ratio?
The short answer is yes.
Consider this:

Compared with Company A’s 5%, Company B’s 7% dividend yield is higher.
However, Company B is paying out more than what it earns with a 140% dividend payout ratio.
This puts pressure on its financial resources and increases the risk of future dividend cuts.
For a real-world case of a high yield paired with a stretched payout, consider
ComfortDelGro Corporation Limited
(SGX: C52).
It paid S$0.085 per share in dividends for FY2025.
At its share price of S$1.25 on 16 November 2026, that works out to a dividend yield of 6.8%.
ComfortDelGro paid out 80% of its FY2025 profit as dividends.
However, it kept its 1H2026 interim dividend at S$0.0391 per share even as PATMI (profit after tax and minority interests) fell 19.7% year on year.
With net debt rising to S$1.03 billion as at 30 September 2026, from S$730.1 million at the end of 2025, ComfortDelGro has limited flexibility to increase its payout.
Management, however, expects net gearing of 26.1% to ease by year end, as it typically peaks in the third quarter.
How Should Beginners Use These Two Metrics?
It is not about choosing between dividend yield and payout ratio, but about using both metrics together to get a complete picture when researching dividends.
When evaluating a dividend-paying stock, consider three simple questions:
Is the dividend yield attractive relative to the risks?
Is the company earning enough to support its dividend payments?
Has the company maintained or increased its dividends over time?
If the answer to all three questions is yes, you might have identified a promising dividend stock.
If any answer is no, treat it as a warning sign of an unsustainable payout or a yield trap, which we will cover in the next article of this series.
Ultimately, dividend metrics are not a standalone reason to invest, but a starting point for deeper research.
Get Smart: Look Beyond the Yield
While dividend yield measures annual dividend income relative to the share price, the payout ratio shows how much of a company’s earnings are distributed to shareholders.
A high dividend yield is only attractive if it is financially sustainable.
Rather than treating these metrics as an either-or, investors should evaluate them together to assess a dividend stock’s true potential.

title: Huawei found guilty of US criminal charges in landmark case
article:
(Nov 25): Huawei Technologies Co, China’s largest technology company, was found guilty of multiple US criminal charges, including money laundering, a conspiracy to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran and North Korea.

A federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, deliberated for about four days before reaching a verdict Tuesday in a rare US prosecution of a foreign corporation. The panel found the company guilty of 10 of 12 counts following an 11-week trial. Huawei was cleared of two conspiracy charges related to racketeering and obstruction of justice.

The verdict against one of China’s biggest and best-known tech giants lands at a delicate time for relations between the world’s largest economies, with the Trump administration tightening curbs on China’s ability to access American chips after revelations that Nvidia Corp’s Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence.

Even so, the years-old case is unlikely to affect the broader trade truce between leaders Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, who affirmed a commitment to keep ties stable in a summit last week. While that deal is set to expire in January, both sides have an incentive to prevent a deterioration that could lead to much higher tariffs and bans on essential items like rare earths, airplane parts and chip design software.

“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws,” said Brooklyn US Attorney Joseph Nocella. “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes years-long collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies.”

Brian Heberlig, Huawei’s lead lawyer, focused on the company’s acquittal on two charges, including the so-called RICO racketeering count, which he called the government’s lead charge. The company said in a separate statement that the remaining charges have no merit and it will review its legal options.

See also: Ex-RBI chief Rajan sees Nvidia governance risk with return of Huang

“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig said. The RICO charge “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”

The decision comes years after the Justice Department first filed charges against the world’s largest maker of telecommunications equipment. For most of that time, the company has been largely excluded from the American market under trade measures imposed by the Trump and Biden administrations in the name of national security.

See also: Australia bolsters online safety law with tougher Big Tech fine

The telecom titan has emerged as China’s de facto national chipmaking champion and is one of a handful of firms central to Beijing’s goal of dominating artificial intelligence and replacing American software and circuitry with local equivalents.

The case was publicly unveiled in early 2019 under the first Trump administration’s so-called China Initiative, a Justice Department programme to combat Chinese espionage and influence in the US. Prosecutors have since won numerous convictions against Chinese nationals, but have struggled in trials against large Chinese companies on American soil.

The jury of nine women and three men heard testimony from more than 60 witnesses during the 11-week trial. Huawei was convicted of a scheme to steal trade secrets from rival tech competitors during a 20-year period, including source code from Cisco Systems Inc, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile as well as proprietary information from Fujitsu Network Communications.

“Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion, and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies, they are serious crimes,” said James Barnacle, head of the FBI’s New York office. “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”

In their verdict Tuesday, however, the panel rejected the government’s theory that Huawei had engaged in a racketeering scheme for more than two decades to “grow its global brand” into one of the biggest telecoms in the world.

The panel also rejected a US charge that Huawei obstructed a federal grand jury investigation. Jurors left the courthouse and declined to speak to the press.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The conviction is a vindication for the Justice Department, which overcame attempts by Huawei to derail the case before trial and had to navigate years of delays because of the Covid pandemic, which made it difficult for lawyers and witnesses to travel. Along the way, two Chinese intelligence officers were accused in 2022 of trying to bribe a US law enforcement official with US$61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and get inside information about the case.

Huawei now faces fines, forfeiture and restitution but the US has not specified the scope of financial penalties it will seek at sentencing, which is scheduled for September 2027.

From the beginning, the Huawei case heightened tensions between Washington and Beijing while the world’s two largest economies were mired in a trade war. Months later, officials in Donald Trump’s administration labelled the company a national security threat, alleging that it sold telecommunications equipment that could be used by China’s Communist Party for spying.

The initial criminal indictment set off a diplomatic crisis when Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou, whose father founded the company, was arrested at the behest of the US on financial fraud charges while travelling through Canada. Almost three years after Meng was held under house arrest in Vancouver, she reached a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021 that allowed her to return to China, but after she admitted that the company violated US sanctions by illegally conducting business in Iran.

title: Shein to pay US$100 mil to end US deceptive marketing case
article:
(Nov 25): Shein Global Holdings Ltd agreed to pay US$100 million ($129 million) to resolve US Federal Trade Commission allegations that the Chinese fast-fashion retailer deceived consumers about its products, suppliers and consumer reviews.

In a complaint filed in California federal court, the FTC alleged Shein violated US consumer protection laws by failing to provide adequate customer service, illegally screening consumer reviews and misrepresenting the country of origin and labour practices of its suppliers. The antitrust and consumer protection agency seeks an injunction and monetary relief for consumers harmed by the company’s allegedly illegal practices.

The terms of the settlement, including the US$100 million payment, which will be used to reimburse consumers, were also filed in federal court.

In a statement, the company said it had reached an agreement to resolve the investigation, which it said related to “certain historical business practices”. The company also said that it disagrees with the FTC’s characterisations, but was taking steps to bolster its compliance practices.

Shares of Shein opened largely flat on Wednesday morning in Hong Kong.

For years, Shein had no customer service phone number and, until September 2025, only five agents despite selling millions of packages to the US every day, the FTC said. The company also delayed or refused to publish consumer reviews that contained what it deemed “unhelpful words” such as “damaged”, “bad quality”, “very disappointed” and “waste of money” among others, according to the complaint.

The agency also alleged that Shein failed to substantiate its marketing claims about responsible sourcing or the use of cotton grown by forced labour.

Shein, which had shares listed in Hong Kong on Sept 1, has attracted millions of shoppers in the US and Europe with rock-bottom prices and a torrent of new styles by capitalising on customs duty waivers for small-value parcels. The Trump administration has sought to close that loophole, ending the so-called de minimis exemption that allowed cheap goods to pass through customs tariff-free for nearly 90 years.

Shein’s US sales fell 6.6% in the 12-month period that ended in October, according to Bloomberg Second Measure, which analyses credit and debit card transactions.

See also: Onitsuka Tiger pivots from Asics stripes to tap luxury market

The latest case adds to a growing list of legal and regulatory challenges for Shein in the US. Its purchase of American clothing retailer Everlane triggered a national security review by US authorities earlier this year. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued the company in February, alleging that it unlawfully sold toxic products and exposed Americans’ personal data to the Chinese government.

The retailer has also drawn scrutiny in Western markets over its environmental and labour practices, including cotton tied to China’s Xinjiang region.

Its handling of customer data has come under pressure too. French regulators last year fined Shein roughly €150 million (US$164 million or $212 million) for violating online tracking rules, including by placing advertising cookies on users’ devices without their consent.

Shein’s expansion beyond fashion has brought further headaches. In late 2025, the company came under scrutiny over childlike sex dolls and weapons sold on its third-party marketplace, prompting investigations in France and leaving it at risk of hefty EU penalties. The controversy coincided with strong political pushback to the opening of its first physical store in Paris.

title: AI chip boom to see won build on best year in almost a decade
article:
(Nov 25): South Korea’s AI chip windfall is unleashing a wave of year-end currency flows, potentially pushing the won into its next phase of gains.

SK Hynix Inc and Samsung Electronics Co are poised to convert much of their massive export earnings to pay for dividends and record employee bonuses in won. They will also need more of the local currency to cover large tax bills owed to the government from the artificial intelligence hardware surge.

Those inflows are expected to help boost the won into the 1,200-per-dollar range by the end of the first half of 2027, according to Macro Hive and Korea Investment & Securities. Citing similar catalysts, Goldman Sachs Group Inc sees the currency strengthening to 1,280 next year, a roughly 5% gain from Wednesday’s level of 1,345.80.

Compressed into the next few weeks, these payouts bode well for the won, adding momentum to a 7% gain against the dollar so far this year. While overseas investors repatriating their dividends may create some won-selling pressure in the short term, record exports and a hefty current-account surplus also keep the currency’s 2027 upward trajectory intact, market watchers say.

“The bigger story is that exporters still have substantial dollar-selling needs,” said Vivek Rajpal, Asia strategist at JB Drax Honore in Singapore. “The won’s appreciation trend has further to go despite weak sentiment towardsAI stocks.”

See also: Alibaba in talks for potential yuan, dollar bond sale next year — Bloomberg

The won has rallied about 16% since hitting a 17-year low in June, as exporters led by chipmakers stepped up dollar sales to fund projects in Korea. The currency is outperforming all its Asian peers this year and heading for its biggest annual gain since 2017.

Korea’s two largest chipmakers are rolling out unprecedented dividend plans, driven by a memory-chip sales bonanza and a government push for local firms to boost shareholder returns.

Samsung is scheduled to distribute 30 trillion won (US$22.3 billion) in third-quarter cash dividends on Nov 27, which is about 12 times the average size of its quarterly payouts since the beginning of 2025, according to filings.

See also: Foxconn faces India insolvency lawsuit over unpaid vendor dues — Bloomberg

SK Hynix will pay its 14.1 trillion won dividend allocation for the quarter roughly by the end of the year, or more than 50 times the average size of its quarterly payouts since the beginning of 2025, company filings show.

The payouts should support the won, said Moon Dawoon, an economist at Korea Investment & Securities. Companies are likely to convert more dollars into won to fund the payouts than what will ultimately flow back out as foreign investors repatriate their proceeds, she said.

To be sure, a large share of the cash will go to overseas shareholders, who tend to swiftly convert payouts back into greenbacks.

Foreign investors are estimated to receive about 15 trillion won from Samsung, while SK Hynix’s foreign investors are also slated to receive about half of its total payouts, according to Bloomberg calculations based on share ownership data.

In total, Samsung’s foreign investors will repatriate about half of the dividends they receive, amounting to about $5 billion, as they’ve typically done in the past, estimated Lee Minhyeok, an economist at Kookmin Bank.

Those outflows could bite harder toward year-end as global funds close their books and average trading volumes thin, a backdrop compounded by a stronger dollar and a pullback in semiconductor stocks, Lee said.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“There is considerable downside pressure” on the won this week ahead of the payouts, Lee said, referring to those from Samsung due Nov 27. “Some investors may convert their proceeds into dollars more quickly than usual to lock in their returns,” he added, while still expecting the won to rally in the longer-term period.

The chip boom is also set to deliver record worker bonuses early next year, potentially prompting chipmakers to sell more dollars to fund the won payouts.

Major chip, auto and shipbuilding companies will pay 60 trillion to 70 trillion won in bonuses in 2027, roughly six times this year’s 10.9 trillion won, according to Bank of Korea’s estimates.

Samsung and SK Hynix typically pay annual incentives in the first quarter, and the central bank estimated they alone will account for about 60 trillion won in the first three months of the year.

Bonus payments are likely to generate some temporary volatility in won trading, said Mingze Wu, a currency trader at StoneX Financial. “But overall the prevalent trend of the day will likely stay,” Wu added. Bonuses and special payments are “likely to be spaced out.”

Companies with December fiscal years must pay corporate taxes by the end of March, forcing exporters to raise won ahead of the deadline.

Thanks to a semiconductor-driven windfall, the Korean government projects record corporate tax revenue of 478.6 trillion won for 2026, up 28% from last year. Tax payments will contribute about $102 billion in net won demand and help lift the currency to 1,200 per dollar by mid-2027, Macro Hive estimates.

The chipmakers’ taxes and bonuses will be “a big deal,” JB Drax’s Rajpal said.

title: Banks put data centre clients under microscope on AI chips — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 25): Banks from Citigroup Inc to Standard Chartered plc have launched sweeping reviews of data centre clients in the wake of tougher American rules to curb Chinese companies’ use of advanced US chips in Southeast Asian nations.

The banks join major Asian lenders — including Singapore’s DBS Group Holdings Ltd, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp and United Overseas Bank Ltd — in pushing for more disclosures from companies tied to data centres in Singapore, Malaysia and other countries in the region, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

The banks are pressing clients for further details on who uses their chips and seeking proof they’re in line with stricter export-control rules enacted by the US Commerce Department, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the queries are confidential. A key focus has been neocloud companies that stockpile chips and lease out computing power, with private equity firms, major players in financing Asia’s data centre boom, also receiving questions, the people said.

“We have reached out to our customers to understand the implications of the new rules,” Pauline Ho, OCBC’s group chief credit officer for wholesale banking, said in a statement. “Based on our engagement to date, we do not anticipate material concerns at this juncture, given that the vast majority of our data centre exposure is to US hyperscalers. We will continue to monitor developments closely.”

The industry sweep shows the key role that global banks will play in cracking down on diversions of US chips after the recent scandal involving Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang put the spotlight on the black market for US chips.

Standard Chartered, as well as banks operating in Singapore, are keeping the Monetary Authority of Singapore in the loop on their findings, the people said.

See also: Trump threatens to tax firms building data centres abroad

“MAS expects financial institutions to remain vigilant and assess the risks arising from their activities and exposures,” the Singapore financial regulator said in a statement.

Standard Chartered declined to comment. While the UK bank had been angling to increase its financing of Asian data centres and has been actively looking at graphics-processing unit deals for the past two years, it has been less aggressive than peers amid changing US regulations.

Wall Street has already been tightening lending standards as banks struggle to absorb a wave of artificial intelligence-related debt and cope with growing public opposition to US data centre projects. The new scrutiny raises the possibility that some older bank loans will be found in breach of covenants, forcing backers to wrestle with potential losses.

See also: Nextdc says it will no longer develop data centres near homes

Loan exposure to data centres at DBS, OCBC and UOB accounts for a low-single-digit percentage of their total loan book as of the latest quarter, according to the lenders’ figures.

“Standard financing terms include warranties of compliance with applicable and prevailing domestic and international laws — any responsible bank would work with customers to understand how this is achieved,” DBS, Singapore’s largest lender, said in a statement. “DBS remains committed to supporting our data centre customers and continues to work on data centre financing transactions, subject to applicable regulatory requirements across jurisdictions.”

A UOB spokesperson said that the bank regularly reviews its financing portfolio and is engaging with clients on the new US rules. A representative for Citigroup declined to comment.

Nvidia, whose advanced chips and other products have helped power the AI boom, reinstated Huang as CEO this week, despite revelations of his affair with Alice Huang. Megaspeed International, her former company, is now on a US blacklist that bars it from buying advanced AI chips following allegations that it may have been smuggling Nvidia’s products into China.

The scandal brought attention to the networks linking Nvidia, Chinese customers and middlemen operating in overseas data centres. Nvidia is at the centre of multiple US probes over how China was able to harness its coveted chips. Some bankers now wonder, however, whether shifting political winds could eventually lead the US to ease chip-export restrictions on China.

For now they’re leaning into a bigger oversight role. The Commerce Department is requiring data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand to obtain licences to buy advanced chips made in the US, closing a loophole that allowed the silicon to reach mainland China. In Singapore, a global financial hub that’s played a key role in financing data centres being built across Southeast Asia, the rules threaten to cool growth.

“We do not enforce America’s export controls, but we do not want Singapore to be used and abused as a conduit by companies to circumvent America’s export controls,” Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Tuesday. The city-state will facilitate US checks while taking “very firm enforcement actions” against companies that breach local law, he said.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Banks in Southeast Asia, especially Singapore and Malaysia, are among the biggest funders of China-linked data centres and would take a hit should Chinese tenants leave, according to a Natixis report.

For deals in the works, US banks added new language to financing documents after the export controls were tightened. And lenders have frozen work on a US$480 million ($619 million) loan that would have funded Nvidia chips for use by China’s ByteDance, Bloomberg reported last week.

The scrutiny from banks is creating additional pressure for neoclouds. The new class of AI companies was already struggling with heavy debt loads and increasingly had to scrape together financial backstops from deep-pocketed tech firms to secure data centre capacity.

“You’re talking about placing limits on the ultimate use of the compute, which potentially makes certain projects less valuable and less resilient,” said Andrew Caridas, a partner at the law firm Ashurst Perkins Coie. “That’s going to be a concern.”

title: Alibaba in talks for potential yuan, dollar bond sale next year — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 25): Chinese e-commerce and cloud services giant Alibaba Group Holding Ltd has been in discussions in recent weeks with banks about potentially raising money in the offshore bond markets next year, people familiar with the matter said.

The company has held initial talks with investment banks to evaluate a potential sale of notes possibly in offshore yuan and dollars, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. Deliberations are preliminary and details could change. Borrowers weigh factors including market volatility in ultimately deciding on the timing for any offerings.

The group would join a growing number of tech firms that have been tapping capital markets to raise the trillions of dollars needed to finance AI infrastructure, testing how far investor demand can go. In October, Chinese technology and gaming company Tencent Holdings Ltd raised almost US$5.7 billion from the sale of bonds in yuan and dollars to support its growing investments in artificial intelligence.

Ahead of any potential overseas bond deal, Alibaba has been working on getting a quota for such issuance from the National Development and Reform Commission, the people said.

See also: Foxconn faces India insolvency lawsuit over unpaid vendor dues — Bloomberg

The company reported quarterly earnings last week, revealing an acceleration in capital expenditures to sustain its AI ambitions. Despite having successfully raised US$10.2 billion through a record-breaking Hong Kong share placement in August, its capital spending for the third quarter rose 60% from a year ago to about 50.5 billion yuan (US$7.6 billion), driven by faster computing scaling and the hardware buildout required for its Qwen AI models and expected AI agent adoption.The company has said it’s facing higher costs for chip components, a direct side effect of navigating US export controls and restricted supply chains. To counter these hardware bottlenecks, Alibaba had committed more than US$53 billion over a three-year period to build a full suite of services and businesses from models to chips.

To fund its push for semiconductor independence, Alibaba plans to list its chip-design unit, T-Head, in Hong Kong. The spinoff would give T-Head direct access to capital markets to develop domestic alternatives to US hardware.

title: Asian stocks fall as AI trade falters, gold drops
article:
(Nov 25): Asian stocks retreated after a sell-off in US technology shares revived doubts about the durability of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, extending losses from Wall Street into the region. Gold fell.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index slipped 2%, giving up some gains from Tuesday’s rally that was the biggest since July. The Kospi Index in South Korea lost 4.5% and the Taiwanese benchmark 5% as the two key barometers of the AI trade in Asia came under pressure. Futures for the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 indices both fell at least 0.4%.

Precious metals sold off as gold fell for a seventh time in eight sessions to around US$3,550 an ounce. Treasuries added to gains from the New York session when investors sought the safety of fixed income amid the losses in stocks. The yield on the benchmark 10-year note slipped one basis point to 4.92%.

The volatility in stocks underscore the uncertainty surrounding the AI trade as investors question whether massive technology spending can generate sufficient returns. Attention is now turning to Wednesday’s US inflation reading, which may affect the Federal Reserve’s policy path, and a possible tariff announcement from the Trump administration.

“This is so dizzying day to day,” said Adam Phillips, managing director of portfolio strategy at EP Wealth Advisors, who is not buying the dip in stocks yet. “Nothing has significantly changed from Monday, but we’re not out of the woods yet. There is still a whole lot of fear and uncertainty around the AI trade that needs to be worked through.”

Traders are parsing the Trump administration’s push to replace levies struck down by the Supreme Court. The US is set to announce as soon as late Tuesday in Washington plans to raise tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and more than a dozen other economies, according to people familiar with the matter.

See also: Asian stocks jump as Huang’s return lifts AI trade

The additional tariffs won’t push overall rates above levels agreed in individual trade deals, including pacts US President Donald Trump negotiated with the EU and China, people familiar with the details said. Still, the renewed focus on tariffs revived concerns about the potential impact on economic growth, corporate profits and inflation.

“The news of potential new US tariffs is probably mostly baked into market expectations at this point,” said Frederic Neumann, chief Asia economist at HSBC Holdings plc. “The US administration has been working for a while to replace some of the tariffs struck down by judges earlier this year, and its efforts have been well telegraphed.”

Investors remain focused on AI and the Fed into year-end, Neumann said.

See also: Asian stocks fall as Anthropic slips in after-hours

Stocks have swung back and forth in the past three sessions. Friday witnessed a selloff as the AI trade cratered, while equities bounced back on Monday as Jensen Huang returned to the helm of Nvidia Corp. Some of those gains were lost on Tuesday as Nvidia sank 5.9%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index tumbled 7.9% Tuesday, taking its decline from a June peak to about 40%. Anthropic PBC traded below its IPO price. Shares of Dell Technologies Inc and HP Inc edged up in extended trading after they issued upbeat forecasts.

“What the market is telling us is that investors do not believe that this amount of investment probably can proceed as they are guided previously, at least not in a sustainable way,” Dong Chen, chief investment officer Asia at Bank J Safra Sarasin, said on Bloomberg Television.

In other corners of the market, oil slipped as traders weighed signs of rising supply against escalating attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude fell 0.7% to US$90.75 a barrel.

Investors also parsed fresh US economic data that showed US consumer confidence surged to the highest in nearly two years. The report came ahead of the Fed’s preferred inflation metric, which is seen adding to bets that officials will raise interest rates in December.

Even as the Fed tightens policy, Treasuries will continue to advance over the next year, according to Joe Maher at Capital Economics.

“The tech-driven rout in the stock market has further to run and will prompt investors to revise down their rate expectations and trigger a ‘flight-to-safety’ into bonds,” he said.

title: Foxconn faces India insolvency lawsuit over unpaid vendor dues — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 25): About half a dozen vendors in India are experiencing payment delays by Foxconn Technology Group’s local unit, said people familiar with the matter, with one even filing an insolvency lawsuit to recover US$15 million in unpaid dues.

BCD Emprasa LLP, which leased dormitory housing in southern India for the Foxconn unit’s employees at the Bengaluru facility, has alleged that it didn’t receive payment for rent and utilities in an Aug 12 petition to the National Company Law Tribunal’s Chennai bench.

The company is seeking about 1.43 billion rupees (US$15.3 million) for past dues along with interest, service charges and damages as of July 8 from Foxconn Hon Hai Technology India Mega Development Pvt Ltd, according to the filing, which was seen by Bloomberg News.

Vendors in India often initiate insolvency proceedings to recover overdue payments, though these filings rarely push a company into bankruptcy.

While the dispute isn’t expected to derail Foxconn’s growth plans in India, it adds to the challenges facing the iPhone assembler as it competes with Tata Electronics Pvt Ltd for a bigger role in Apple Inc’s supply chain. Bloomberg News reported last year that Foxconn recalled hundreds of Chinese workers from India — though the reason wasn’t clear at the time — in a move that saw the company bring in staff from Taiwan and Vietnam to minimize the impact on production.

Foxconn didn’t reply to emailed queries seeking comments on BCD’s lawsuit in India.

See also: Intesa opens US$36 bil bid on world’s oldest bank to investors

“These defaults have caused grave financial prejudice and substantial commercial harm to the company” BCD said in an emailed response, adding that the matter was sub judice before NCLT.

At least four vendors other than BCD have been waiting for several months to over a year for Foxconn to clear their dues, said people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private information.

Several were hired for construction-related work on the Bengaluru facility and were working with Foxconn for the first time.

See also: Coca-Cola HBC rises in JSE debut ahead of US$2.6 bil deal

Under an April 2024 agreement with BCD, Foxconn leased 700 residential units for female employees, with rent payable regardless of occupancy and a lock-in through July 2026, according to the NCLT filing. Foxconn defaulted on an invoice due in May 2025, it said. The electronics giant also did not agree to appointing an arbitrator.

Departures of some non-Indian staff have slowed payments to local contractors, the people said.

title: Koh Eco’s subsidiary ordered to pay $30.1 mil to its joint venture partner following arbitration proceeding
article:
Back on Aug 18, Koh Brothers Eco’s (Koh Eco) wholly-owned subsidiary, Koh Brothers Building & Civil Engineering (KBCE) has commenced an arbitration proceeding against its joint venture partner, which is a construction and engineering company, in respect of a construction project.

Following which, the arbitral tribunal has issued its final award on Nov 24, which ordered KBCE to pay its joint venture partner a total amount of $30.1 million within 28 days.

With this development, Koh Eco is evaluating the various options with its legal advisors, including whether to ask the court to cancel or nullify the final award.

Nonetheless, Koh Eco expects the final award to have a material impact on its net tangible assets and earnings (loss) per share for FY2026 ending Dec 31.

“However, taking into account the overall financial position and liquidity, the board does out expect the final award to give rise to a material uncertainty that would cast significant doubt on the group's ability to continue as a going concern,” reads the Nov 25 announcement.

Koh Eco has been in the news recently following its Mainboard transfer, announcing plans to raise gross proceeds of up to $27.6 mil via rights issue at 4.9 cents each.

As at 9.25am, shares of Koh Eco were trading 0.2 cents lower, or down 4.26% at 4.5 cents.

title: iX Biopharma aims to raise at least $14 mil by placing new shares at 39.8 cents each
article:
iX Biopharma announced it plans to raise at least $14 million by placing out roughly 35.18 million new shares at a placement price of 39.8 cents. The new shares represent around 3.1% of the enlarged share base.

At 39.8 cents, it represents a discount of 9% to the volume weighted average price of 43.72 cents for trades done on Nov 24.

iX Biopharma explains that the latest placement will provide funding to drive the development of Wafermine as well as the group’s expansion into the US through the compounding pharmacy pathway.

iX Biopharma intends to allocate 48% of the net proceeds raised from the placement for the development of its consumer and compounding business, including potential strategic investments, acquisitions or partnerships.

19% of the net proceeds will be allocated for the development and commercialisation of Wafermine while the remaining 33% will be used for general working capital.

Assuming iX Biopharma could raise more than $14 million from this placement, the group intends to utilise the additional proceeds towards potential strategic acquisitions, investments or business development opportunities.

title: Beng Kuang Marine CEO Yong lifts shareholding above 5%
article:
Beng Kuang Marine CEO Yong Jiunn Run has become a substantial shareholder of his company after exercising 3,045,000 warrants into new ordinary shares at an exercise price of $0.22 per share, for a total consideration of $669,900.

Yong now holds 5.09% interest in Beng Kuang, up from the previous 4.13%.

Beng Kuang executive chairman Chua Beng Yong says that he is “gratified” that Yong has increased his shareholding in Beng Kuang and further and aligning his interests closer with the firm’s shareholders.

Chua adds: “Since taking the helm as CEO, Yong has spearheaded a significant turnaround and strategic transformation of the group, delivering tangible results and enhancing value for shareholders. With the ‘Beng Kuang 2.0’ roadmap taking shape, I am confident that Yong’s leadership and commitment as both CEO and shareholder will continue to drive the group’s next phase of growth and value creation.”

Under Yong’s leadership and his “Beng Kuang 2.0” roadmap, Beng Kuang has achieved a turnaround, strengthening the balance sheet through non-core divestments, exiting underperforming businesses and reducing gearing.

The company has transformed its business model to focus on higher-growth, cash-generative infrastructure engineering and corrosion prevention services, becoming an asset-light and service-centric solutions provider specialised engineering, maintenance and regulatory compliance solutions for the marine and offshore energy sectors.

See also: Senior insiders spend on Wilmar, Mi Material and Stamford Land Corporation shares

Earnings quality has also improved, mostly coming from recurring FPSO lifecycle activities. The firm has consolidated subsidiary Asian Sealand Offshore and Marine while incubating new business opportunities to position the company for its next phase of growth.

More significantly, after returning to profitability in FY2023, shareholders were rewarded with the resumption of dividends and issuance of free warrants.

Shares in Beng Kuang closed at 29.5 cents on Nov 24, down 0.5 cents or 1.7%

title: Soaring US steel prices drive ‘mad scramble’ for imported tons
article:
(Nov 25) : Cheaper Asian imports are gaining traction with US steel buyers despite Washington’s tariffs, as a data center construction boom squeezes domestic supplies and drives up prices.

President Donald Trump’s 50% levies have sharply curtailed foreign steel shipments into the US. But with domestic prices of the metal reaching four-year highs, cheaper supply from East Asian sellers has flowed into the country in recent months.

Imports of South Korea’s flat-rolled steel surged 68% through October compared with the same period in 2025, according to data compiled by the American Iron and Steel Institute. October applications for steel from Vietnam more than doubled from September’s final import volumes, reaching 213,000 net tons and making it the fourth-largest foreign supplier that month.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and its needed power infrastructure has juiced up US demand for steel beyond expectations. The rush of projects — which use steel in anything from laying a building’s foundation to server racks and ductwork — is straining domestic supply, with steel orders booking up fast and US mills struggling to fulfill demand.

“There’s a mad scramble for tons,” said Timna Tanners, an analyst at Wells Fargo. “The US mills are not giving buyers enough steel — they’re cutting back on their supply agreements into 2027.”

The steady return of foreign imports reveals the limits of the Trump administration’s tariffs, which were designed to make foreign material prohibitively expensive and insulate domestic producers, like Nucor Corp., Steel Dynamics Inc. and Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. Persistent demand for steel has driven US prices to a height where foreign sellers can now afford the associated levies.

See also: Nasdaq 100 falls 2% on AI rout, tariff hike talk

Some imported steel can be nearly US$400 a ton cheaper than domestic supplies even after accounting for tariffs and shipping costs, according to a recent note from Jefferies analyst Albert Realini.

This week, Nucor, the largest American steel producer, raised its advertised price for hot-rolled coil to US$1,330 a short ton, extending a run of weekly increases that began during the summer. Hot-rolled coil, which is used to make products ranging from cars to construction materials, is the most widely traded form of steel.

Broader market prices have also climbed with US hot-rolled steel recently quoted at more than US$1,300 a ton, compared with less than US$900 a year earlier.

See also: US blacklists Megaspeed, and six firms across Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand over chip diversion risk

“Import volumes have been increasing in recent months, including a massive surge from South Korea,” Leon Topalian, Nucor’s chief executive officer, said during the company’s late-October earnings call. “But make no mistake, demand is very healthy. Even as imports have crept higher this year, domestic shipments have risen in each of the past three quarters.”

American mills have ramped up production as prices climbed and foreign supplies dwindled. US steel output rose 5.9% through the week ending Nov. 14 from a year earlier, according to the American Iron and Steel Institute. But the higher output hasn’t alleviated supply constraints, with mill outages, strong order books and declining imports limiting the amount of steel readily available to buyers.

For small manufacturers like Marlin Steel, which makes custom products from steel wire and sheet metal, that can mean a longer wait for orders.

Drew Greenblatt, CEO of Marlin Steel, says he only buys from American producers, and the orders he places with steel mills are now taking between eight and 12 weeks to fill, rather than the one- to three-day shipment time his company enjoyed a year ago. In turn, Greenblatt says his company has stocked up on inventory.

“It’s very awkward for us to have to reframe our pricing to our clients,” he said. “So I try to overbuy now so that I can keep shipping volumes to them. We’ve been buying a lot more than we really need.”

In Korea, the steel industry is dominated by giants like POSCO Holdings and Hyundai Steel Co., which have substantial capacity to produce metal and have searched for overseas markets as demand at home remains sluggish. Vietnam, meanwhile, has rapidly expanded its steelmaking capacity in recent years, supplying everything from construction steel and hot-rolled coil to pipes and galvanized sheets.

That shift has alarmed domestic producers, who have long complained about competitors from Asia that they say use the US as a dumping ground.

US steelmakers in September urged the Trump administration to investigate a surge in South Korean shipments, pointing to sharp increases in imports of construction steel, pipes and flat-rolled products. Korean steel shipments reached 519,000 tons in September alone, up 21% from August, while imports from Japan jumped 60%.

The US market is “undeniably in the midst of a significant squeeze driven by a combination of low end-customer inventory, data center demand, and seasonal restocking,” Alexander Hacking, a Citigroup analyst, wrote in a note to clients. “When this squeeze alleviates remains to be seen.”

title: Nasdaq 100 falls 2% on AI rout, tariff hike talk
article:
(Nov 25) : Wall Street’s doubts about the durability of the artificial-intelligence trade spurred selling in technology stocks, with investors also parsing talks of fresh US tariffs.

Just a day after an AI-led surge, the Nasdaq 100 sank 2%. Nvidia Corp. lost about 6%. Anthropic PBC dropped below its IPO price. While the S&P 500 edged lower, most of its firms rose. In late hours, HP Inc. and Dell Technologies Inc. gave solid outlooks.

“While we believe that the low point for stocks during this recent volatility has already been reached, we still expect continued chop as this market remains very headline-sensitive when it comes to AI,” said Rick Gardner at RGA Investments.

Fears over AI safety emerged after Axios reported that some Anthropic and OpenAI unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released.

Meantime, the US is set to announce plans to raise tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and more than a dozen other economies, according to people familiar with the matter.

However, the additional tariffs won’t lead to an overall rate that exceeds the agreed-upon levels in individual trade deals, including the pacts President Donald Trump negotiated with the EU and China, people familiar with the details said.
